senses: To make cheerful or merry.
examples: When in the oration ther is nothing rightly and properly spoken, but all is to muche befigured and begayed.
I find it the finest land & folk yet, finer even than Denmark & the Danes, though truly not so begaying & behopefulling.

senses: A large flowing Arab cloak.
Someone devoted to hedonism.
To introduce samples into a mass spectrometer using such a device
A proponent of contextualism, or the importance of context.
examples: He is more of a contextualist, believing that “letters are fluid, that they change with time and circumstance — the entire word is more important than a single letter, and its form can fluctuate.”

senses: Heavily forested ground in the Amazon basin.
ety: Borrowed from Portuguese selva, from Latin silva. Doublet of silva.

senses: A person suffering from ataxia.
A West and South Asian sweet drink prepared from fruits or flower petals; a sherbet.
ety: Borrowed from Hindustani, from Classical Persian شَرْبَت (šarbat). Doublet of sherbet and sorbet.
examples: When Mrs. Dwivedi had no longer felt like standing there tracking Chellam's progress in the punishing heat, she’d come indoors, ordered her cook to make her a tall glass of iced sharbat, and telephoned Amma.

senses: The process or act of making more liberal.
examples: Paisley's three year "Save Ulster from Sodomy" campaign has been a significant force in preventing until now the liberalization of laws about gayness in the British protectorate.

senses: A group of organisms having the same genetic constitution.
The psychological symptom in which the world appears to be unreal, and the patient has a sense of detachment from it.
making unreal, in general; detachment from reality or realness.
The loosening of the bonds of (an electron) so that it can move freely among a group of atoms; delocalization.
ety: From de- + real + -ization, or from derealize + -ation.
examples: Derealization frequently co-occurs with depersonalization disorder, in which affected individuals notice an altered perception of their surroundings, resulting in the world seeming unreal or dreamlike.

senses: An area of volcanic activity that gives off sulfurous steam.
ety: From Italian solfatara (“a place where to find sulphates”), from solfato (“sulphate”) + -ara (“suffix that forms place nouns”). More at Italian zolfo (“sulphur”). Itself the name of Solfatara, a volcano near Naples. Compare Sicilian surfatara.
examples: Under these solfataras, (which, at each eruption from the volcano, emitted greater quantities of hot steams) are several hot wells, close to the high-water mark, which, however, seem not to be in the least sulphureous.
Holmes calls these active vents solfataras, so evidently we are at the type locality for this kind of thing.
Vents that produce steam alone are fumaroles, or solfataras if laden with sulphur; impressive, but rarely exciting, they are more common on drier volcanoes than in hydrothermal basins.

senses: Traditional Indian footwear, essentially consisting of a sole with a post and knob engaged between the big toe and second toe.
ety: From a Sanskrit word, derived from the word for "foot".
examples: These natural-rubber sandals are based on the paduka or toe-knob sandals, a 5,000-year-old Indian shoe design.

senses: Natural affection or love, especially of parents for their children.
ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek στοργή (storgḗ, “affection, love (especially of parents and children)”), from στέργω (stérgō, “to love (chiefly of non-sexual affection); to show affection”) (from Proto-Indo-European *sterg- (“to cover; to protect”)) + -η (-ē, suffix forming action nouns).

senses: One who operates a barbecue pit. Sometimes a term of respect for someone who is skilled at barbecuing.
The act of making symmetric.
A tree-lined avenue, often particularly one that is part of a landscaped garden.
examples: He found her walking slowly up and down an allee of elms, through the leaves of which the bright September sunshine sifted down.
About $800,000 for a complete interior and exterior remodeling and about $200,000 for landscaping, including an allee of mature trees

senses: Something that makes something else shrink.
One who shrinks or recoils.
Something that itself shrinks.
examples: Mr. Druggist, are you a shrinker? Hold a minute now — before getting excited. A late dictionary defines a shrinker in a general sense as one who recoils, or draws back fearfully from something dreaded.
These can be called the Blaster (aggressive), the Shrinker (overly passive), or the Me (effective).

senses: A small donkey, especially when used as a pack animal or one that is feral and lives in the southwestern United States or northern Mexico.
An evasive explanation in the form of multiple excuses.
A detour or route that bypasses an obstacle.
A section of type that is narrower than that of the column it is part of; typically next to an illustration.
A whitlow running around the fingernail but not affecting the bone.
examples: I called them to find out what had happened to my parcel, but all I got was a runaround.

senses: The fleshy false fruit of a wild rose plant (e.g. sweetbrier, dog rose, burnet rose, etc.), containing the achenes or true fruits.
Of a shape similar to a papule.
Consisting of papules; characterized by the presence of papules.
An early three-stringed instrument, somewhat like a simple violin only pear shaped, played with a bow and used in Medieval and the early Renaissance eras.
ety: From Middle French rebec, alteration of rubebe (see English ribibe), from Arabic رَبَاب (rabāb).

senses: In Yoruba culture, a priest of Ifa.
A themed bag of commercial merchandise, available at shows (fairs or carnivals) in Australia.
The seeds of this plant, used as a spice (especially in Indian and Thai cooking).
A puzzle in which cells of a grid must be filled or left blank, according to sets of numbers given at the side of the grid, to reveal a hidden picture.
A scarecrow, generally made of feathers tied to a string, hung up to prevent deer from breaking into a place.
ety: From Early Middle English sheueles (“scarecrow”) [and other forms]; probably from Old English *scīewels, from sċīen (“to be frightened or startled; to recoil in fear”) (from Proto-West Germanic *skiuhijan (“to dread; to avoid, shun”), from Proto-Germanic *skeuhaz (“frightened; bashful, coy, shy, timid; cautious, reserved”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *skewbʰ-, *skūbʰ- (“to drive, move forward, push”) or *(s)kewH- (“to cover; to hide”)) + -els (suffix forming masculine nouns). Doublet of shy. Cognates * Middle English asheuelen, asheulen (verb) * Middle Low German schūwelse * Middle High

senses: A hill, a mountain (especially in the Middle East or North Africa).
ety: Borrowed from French djebel, from Arabic جَبَل (jabal, “mountain”).

senses: A small passerine bird, Fringilla coelebs, of the finch family, found throughout Europe and eastward to Iran and eastern Mediterranean coastlands.
ety: From Middle English chaffynch, chaffynche, caffynche, equivalent to chaff + finch. However, more recently the first element has been argued to derive from the same root as Old English cæfed (“ornamented”) and cæfing (“hair-ornament”), thus meaning "ornamented finch, colourful finch".

senses: A thick salty paste made from fermented soybeans, used in Korean cuisine.
Synonym of burial ground.
A woman in a position of authority, especially one in charge of a geisha house or bar in Japan or East Asia.
A wide version of a papasan, suitable for seating two.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese ママさん, from ママ (mama) with the honorific title さん (san).

senses: An oblong piece of skin from which the pieces for a glove are cut.
ety: Attested since the 1860s, of unclear origin. Perhaps from French tranche.

senses: The political practice of intervening in a sovereign state's affairs.
The idea that a person develops cognition through explicit instruction by others, and not merely by being nurtured and allowed to develop individually.
ety: From French interventionnisme. By surface analysis, intervention + -ism.

senses: A person who performs endoscopies.
In Mahayana Buddhism, the intense ontological aspiration to save all beings by following the bodhisattva path to enlightenment.
The bodhisattva path to nirvana.
ety: From Sanskrit बोधिचित्त (bodhicitta, literally “mind of enlightenment, spirit of awakening”), from बोधि (bodhi, “awakening, enlightenment”) + चित्त (cittá, “mind, spirit, reason”).

senses: A person who keeps Sunday as a day of rest, but does not regard it as representing the Sabbath of the Old Testament of the Bible.
A payment legally due from a parishioner to the parish, because the parishioner's house was built on land, ownership of which would have originally obliged the landowner to pay a tithe to the parish.
ety: Inherited from Middle English dominical (“(adjective) of or pertaining to the Lord’s day or Sunday; (noun) a book containing the liturgy for Sunday (?)”), borrowed from Medieval Latin dominicālis (“of or pertaining to Sunday, dominical”), from Latin dominicus (“of or belonging to a lord or master; (Ecclesiastical Latin) God’s, the Lord’s”) (compare diēs Dominicus (“the day of the Lord, Sunday”)) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives of relationship). senses: A proponent of exceptionalism.
A style of theatrical makeup in which a white actor reddens the face in order to portray a Native American.
ety: From red + face, based on earlier blackface.
